Let us keep this blameless. In hindsight, what would you have done differently?
I would have piloted in one region first. I signed off on four.
And if you had piloted in one, what would that have changed?
We would have caught the blind spot in March instead of June. Regional pricing was never in the model.
So was the model the root cause?
No. The model did what we asked it to do. The root cause was the data, and leaving the second market out was an oversight, not a decision.

Two ground rules before we start, because a post-mortem that turns into a search for the guilty person teaches nobody anything. Rule one: we talk about decisions, not people. A decision made with the information available in March is a reasonable decision, even if it looks foolish in June, and that difference is the whole point of the exercise. Rule two: everybody says one thing they would have done differently, including me. If only the junior people answer that question, the meeting is theater. And a warning about language. There is a difference between the root cause and the first thing you notice. The discount backfired, yes, but the discount is the symptom. The reason nobody caught it for three months is the root cause, and that is the part we are here to fix.

Let me tell you about the question that ends more interviews than any other. Tell me about a decision you would make differently today. Most candidates do one of two things, and both are fatal. Some of them say nothing comes to mind, which reads as either dishonest or incurious. Others confess a disaster and then keep apologizing for four minutes, which reads as fragile. What a senior candidate does is shorter than both. Name the decision in one sentence, without defending it. Say what you would have done differently, also in one sentence. Then, and this is the part that wins the room, say what you do differently now because of it. Notice that the last sentence is in the present. If your whole answer stays in the past, you have described a wound. If it ends in the present, you have described a lesson.

First, he names the decision without defending it. Then he says what he would have done differently, in one sentence. After that, he explains what that change would have prevented. Next, he separates the root cause from the symptom. Finally, he says what he does differently today because of it.
